WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Implementation of RGGVY in Bihar and Maharashtra 
*281. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of villages electrified under the Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran 
Yojana during the last two years in Bihar and Maharashtra, district-wise; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the implementation of this scheme is not satisfactory in 
these States; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps Government are taking for 100 per cent implementation of this scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) The 
implementing agencies have reported electrification of 8169 un-electrified villages as on 
09.03.2007 in Bihar under Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY) during 
the last two years. District-wise and year-wise number of villages reported electrified in 
Bihar under RGGVY are given in the Statement (See below). 
2 

[19 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
All the projects in Maharashtra are being executed by the State Discom. Against 
the 17 projects sanctioned, tenders have been issued for 7 projects and no award has 
been placed so far by the executing agency. 
(d) The following steps have been taken to expedite rural electrification work: 
• For effective implementation of the project, Rural Electrification  
Corporation (REC) has developed the framework covering the guidelines 
for the formulation of projects, procurement of goods and services for 
projects to be executed on turn key basis including  bidding procedure, 
franchisee implementation, and technical specificat ions for 
equipment/material and construction standards for a doption in project 
implementation/execution. 
• Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) are prepared district-wise for the purpose of 
cohesiveness and better implementation of projects. 
• For speedier and effective implementation of the pr oject, these are 
executed on turnkey basis. 
• States have been advised to set-up district committ ees to monitor the 
progress of rural electrification works. All the St ates implementing 
RGGVY have already notified formation of district committees. 
• The Government of India as also REC, the nodal agen cy for RGGVY, 
are conducting frequent review meetings with all st akeholders, 
including the concerned State Governments, State po wer utilities and 
implementing agencies for expeditious implementatio n of the scheme 
in accordance with the agreed schedules. 
• The Government of india has set up an inter-Ministe rial Monitoring 
Committee which periodically meets to sanction proj ects and review 
progress of implementation. 
• Wherever the State has desired the services of CPSU s for their 
implementation of the scheme, the same have been pr ovided. 139 
districts have been allocated to CPSUs. 
• The States and implementing agencies, namely the St ate Electricity 
Boards, DISCOMS, CPSUs, have nominated their respec tive nodal 
officers who are responsible for implementation of the scheme in their 
jurisdiction.

(d) No, Sir, An aggregate capacity addition of 76,4 60 MW is feasible 
during 11th Plan for the entire country. In Andhra Pradesh 12 projects with 
aggregate capacity of 5443 MW are proposed to be co mmissioned during 
11th Plan. The details are given in the Statement (See below). 
As regards Andhra Pradesh, NTPC has set up a dedicated power station of 1000 
MW at Simhadri. In addition to this, a Regional Pow er Station of Capacity of 
2100 MW at Ramagundam is already in operation in Andhra Pradesh. An ultra 
mega power project of 4000 MW capacity is also prop osed to be set up at 
Krishnapatnam in Andhra Pradesh. 
The total allocation of Andhra Pradesh from Central  Generation Station in 
Southern Region is 2581 MW, which includes 1000 MW of Simhadri. In 
addition to this, 274 MW of power has also been allocated to Andhra Pradesh from 
unallocated quota in Central Generating Station in Southern Region. 
(e) The National Electricity Policy envisages "Power for all by 2012" and 
per capita availability of power to be increased to 1,000 units by 2011 -12. To 
achieve this objective, a total capacity addition o f about 1,00,000 MW is 
required during 10th and 11th Plan Period. In the 1 0th Plan the capacity 
addition is expected to be 23,250 MW. Strengthening  of inter-State and 
inter-regional transmission system has also been pl anned with hybrid system 
consisting of high voltage DC, ultra high voltage A C (765kv) and extra high 
voltage AC (400kv) lines. It has been proposed to e nhance the inter-regional 
transfer capacity from 11,500 MW at present to 37,0 0 MW by the end of 
2011-12. This will enable transfer of power from su rplus areas to deficit 
areas and ensure optimum utilization of the availab le resources and even 
handed development of the power sector all over the country. 
6 

[19 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Besides, a series of ultra mega power projects with a capacity of 4000 MW 
each have been envisaged in different States. In ad dition to these following 
steps have been taken by the Government to improve power supply position 
in the country:— 
(i) Improving Plant Load Factor (PLF) of existing plants. 
(ii) Rigorous monitoring of production, transportat ion and stocking of 
coal at all major coal based plants in the country to ensure adequate 
availability of fuel to meet the improved PLF of co al stations. 
Import of coal to bridge constraints in production of domestic coal. 
(iii) Tapping of surplus power from captive power plants. 
(iv) Utilization of unutilized capacity of gas based stations on liquid fuel 
as well as purchase of gas from spot market. 
(v) Strengthening/augmentation of sub-transmission system in States 
under Accelerated Power Development Reforms Program me 
(APDRP) as a major step towards reduction of Aggregate Technical 
and Commercial (AT & C) losses. 
(vi) Optimum utilization of available power by strengthening of inter-State 
and inter-regional transmission capacity. 
(vii) Coordinated operation and maintenance of hydr o, thermal, nuclear 
and gas based power stations to optimally utilize t he existing 
generation capacity. 
(viii) Promoting demand side management, energy efficiency and energy 
conservation measures. 
(ix) "Partnership in Excellence" Programme starting with adoption of better 
operation and maintenance (O & M) practices to enable enhancement 
of Plant Load Factor (PLF) of existing thermal power stations through 
tie-up with well performing power utilities as a pr e-cursorto major 
renovation and modernization/life extension.

DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
Will the Minister of FOOD PROCESSING INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the participation of Indi an food processing 
industry in the international market is very unsatisfactory;

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF FOOD 
PROCESSING INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT SAHAI): (a)  to (d) 
According to a study sponsored by Ministry of Food Processing Industries, India's 
exports for agricultural and food products constitutes about 1.6% of total global 
trade. Even though India's export of agricultural a nd food products have been 
on increase, the small percentage of exports in the  global trade is a cause of 
concern. 
The major reasons for unsatisfactory export performance are nonavailability 
of exportable products in adequate quality and quantity, non-tariff barriers in the 
world markets, inability to achieve and maintain high standards of supply as well as 
build a brand image for quality, safety and reliability. 
Government has already taken various initiatives by  providing financial 
assistance to entrepreneurs to bring in modern technology/equipments so as to 
improve quality, cost effectiveness and exportabili ty of their products. 
Government has also been providing assistance for upgrading capacity building 
in HRD, R&D and quality assurance. Moreover, Govern ment has been 
encouraging the exporters for participation in inte rnational fairs/exhibitions for 
better market access, market promotion and showcasing their products. 
As per the Vision 2015 for the food processing sect or adopted by the 
Government, India has the potential to achieve 3% s hare in world trade of 
agricultural and food products by the year 2015. In order to achieve Vision 2015, 
Government has devised various strategies and plans of action to give a boost to 
India's exports of agricultural and food products, some of which are mentioned 
below:— 
(i) To establish supply chains in alignment with in ternational 
requirements by building a strong infrastructural b ase for agri-
business by setting up of Mega Food Parks, Cold Cha in and 
Strategic Distribution Centres in various parts of the country, so as to 
provide a mechanism to bring farmers, processors, retailers together and 
link agricultural production to the market. 
(ii) To undertake capacity building measures for se tting up/ 
upgradation of quality control/food testing laboratories, research

and development and upgradation of skilled manpower to ensure food 
safety and quality matching with international standards. 
(iii) To develop a strong market intelligence syste m including measures 
for supporting brand building, market survey and quality certification to 
aid exporters to identify the target markets and products. 
(iv) To integrate all schemes offered for export pr omotion through 
various Ministries/organizations to gain focused attention.

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (f) The National Programme of Nutritional Support to 
Primary Education (NP-NPSE) is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme for provision of a 
hot cooked meal to children in classes I-V in Government and Government aided 
schools, and Education Guarantee Scheme and Alterna tive and Innovative 
Education Centres under the scheme the Central Gove rnment provides the 
following support: 
1. Free foodgrains through the Food Corporation of India (FCI) 
2. Assistance for cooking cost 
3. Reimbursement of transport subsidy 
4. Assistance for construction of kitchen sheds 
5. Assistance for procurement of kitchen devices 
6. Assistance for Management, Monitoring and Evaluatio n The

the scheme, (i) 450 calories, (ii) 12 grams of proteins, (iii) adequate quantities of

Study on avalanches 
†2107. SHRI JAI PARKASH AGGARWAL: Will the Minister of EARTH 
SCIENCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have conducted or propose to con duct any study 
on national calamities like land slide and avalanch e hitting some parts of the 
country almost every year; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any system is in place to identify such pla ces for 
precautionary measures; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. 
Study of all landslides is undertaken almost every year including recurring type, in 
the northeastern and northwestern Himalayas, northeastern states of the country 
and also in the western ghats/Nilgiri hills in the southern part of India by 
Geological Survey of India (GSI). These are carried out to delineate the tentative 
causative factors and to suggest suitable slope pro tective measures. India 
Meteorblogical Department issues heavy rainfall forecasts which are one of the 
factors leading to land slides. 
Some of the recurring types of landslides studied recently are: 
(i) Sonapur slide on Shillong—Silchar National Highway, Meghalaya; (ii) 9-
Mile slide on NH-31A, Lantakhola slide, B-2 slide, Elachi slide, Serwani slide etc. 
in Sikkim; (iii) Paglajhora slide, Darjeeling, West  Bengal; (iv) Devastating 
Varunavat slide, Uttarkashi, Survee slide, Mussouri, Uttaranchal; (v) Bhilar and 
some other conspicuous slides in Raigarh District of Maharashtra; (vi) Hospital 
slide, Coonoor, Tamil Nadu. 
The study on snow avalanches in India is done by Snow and Avalanche Study 
Establishment (SASE), Defence Research and Developm ent Organization, 
Ministry of Defence. The focus is on helping troops deployed in snow bound 
avalanche prone areas in their day to day movement. All 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2007] 
avalanche prone areas that affect troops movement in western Himalayan region 
have been registered by SASE. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. There are methodologies by wh ich landslide-
vulnerable zones can be demarcated. GS has already completed inventory of about 
1150 landslides spread over north eastern states, n ortheast and north west 
Himalayas, western ghats and Nilgiri hills. GSI is also engaged in carrying cut 
landslide hazard zonation mapping on different scal es to demarcate the 
landslide prone hilly terrain into different zones according to their degree of 
susceptibility to landslides. The main purpose of t his study is to guide the 
planners regarding the land use pattern 
The risk reduction due to avalanches is attempted b y the following 
methods: 
(i) Avalanche Awareness 
(ii) Avalanche Forecasting 
(iii) Avalanche Control 
Regular Avalanche forecasting bulletins are issued from SASE to people living 
in avalanche prone areas about impending danger. Civilian population living in the 
interior region of Himalayas are also informed through Press Information Bureau 
and focal broadcasting stations about the impending danger. 
Study on global warming 
†2108. SHRI JAI PARKASH AGGARWAL: Will the Minister of EARTH 
SCIENCES be pieased to state: 
(a) whether any scientific study on impact of global wa rming on climate 
changes, has been conducted; 
(b) whether various parts of the country have witnessed  such extreme 
conditions of climate such as tsunami, excessive ra ins, and drought because 
of this impact; 
(c) if so, the details of areas most affected by climatic changes; and 
(d) the details of international deliberations on this issue, various aspects 
concerning its prevention, and consensus arrived at various fora to overcome its 
impact? 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
36 

[19 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes, 
Sir. Many scientific studies on global warming and climate change issues have 
been made by the scientists of the India Meteorolog ical. Department and the 
Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The studi es include, long term 
trends of temperature and rainfall over different p arts of the country, changes 
in extreme weather events like heat and cold waves and heavy precipitation 
and trend in tropical cyclone activity over North Indian Ocean. 
(b) and (c) There has been an increase in the extreme weather conditions like 
cyclones, heavy rainfall and drought due to global warming in last 15 years. 
However, no specific change has been noticed in India except a few events like 
Mumbar deluge of 2005 or excessive rainfall in Raja sthan in 2006. During the 
past 100 years, mean temperature over the country (India) has increased by 0.5 C. 
However, there is no appreciable change in the annu al rainfall averaged over 
the country as a whole. 
(d) The Inter-Governmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) working under 
the aegis of the United Nations has submitted its Summary Report on Working 
Group (WG)-I entitled "Climate Change 2007: The Physical Science Basis". 
The main conclusions of the WG-I Panel Report are: 
* Global atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and 
niturous oxide have increased markedly as a result of human activities 
since 1750 and now far exceed pre-industrial values determined from 
ice cores spanning many thousands of years. The giobal increases in 
carbon dioxide concentration are primariiy due to fossil fuel, land-use 
change, while those of methane and nitrous oxide are primarily due 
to agriculture. Wide spread melting of snow and ice, and rising global 
average sea level has been reported. 
* To the report, anthropogenic warming and see level rise would 
continue for centuries due to time scales associate d with climate 
processes and feedbacks, even if greenhouses gas ac cording 
concentrations were to be stabilized.

monitoring of several glaciers during the last 100 years in major basins of Indian 
Himalaya from Shyok in west to Changme Khangpu (Tista) in the East have revealed 
that majority of glaciers in Himalayan region are passing through a phase of recession. 
Observations indicate that during the past 100 years, mean temperature over the 
country (India) as a whole has increased by 0.5°C. 
(b) to (d) GSI has recently initiated study of two glaciers of Bhaga basin viz. 
Mulkila and Yoche Lungpa in July, 2006 which is likely to continue for two more 
years. 
Department of Science and Technology had started an All-India coordinated 
programme on Himalayan glaciers in 1988 with a Prog ramme Advisory and 
Monitoring Committee to study the glaciers of Western and Central Himalaya i.e. 
Gangotri and its tributary glaciers and Chhota Sigri glaciers in Central Himalaya. 
The glacier recession rate varies from glacier to glacier. Preliminary analysis suggests 
the recession rate to be of the order of about 10 t o 15m/ year for some of the 
glaciers. However, long-term data with wider coverage of glaciers are required to 
arrive at a consistent recession rate.

Merchant Power Plants 
2204. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) how far the proposed Merchant Power Plants, where a capacity of 12,000 
MW is envisaged, would be able to meet the target, especially in view of 
prevailing red-tapism; 
(b) if so, whether the power produced by them will form part of national grid 
or each plant wiil have full distribution rights also; and 
(c) if so, whether Government will exercise the price c ontrol mutually 
acceptable and interest of economically weaker sections will be safeguarded? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a ) In 
order to facilitate the development of electricity markets, the Ministry of 
Power has issued an approach paper and guidelines o n development of 
Merchant Power Plants, for which coal linkage/coal blocks allotment would be 
available. Unlike conventional generating plant bou nd by take or pay Power 
Purchase Agreements, Merchant Power Plants compete for customers and 
absorb the full market risk. There are no guarantee s or minimum off-take of 
their output. Typically, the risk of a Merchant Power 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2007] 
Plant is carried on the balance sheet of the promot er. Merchant Power Plants 
can be set up only with the support of the State governments where the plants are 
proposed to be located since the land, water and ot her infrastructure facilities 
required for the power plant need to be provided by the State Government. While 
this initiative is still at a nascent stage, its su ccess, however, would, to a great 
extent, depend on availability of reliable data and information for plant sites and 
other inputs so that the developers then can take further appropriate action to set up 
Merchant Power Plants. 
(b) It is envisaged that MPPs would sell power to bulk consumers/ 
distribution utilities through short term contracts. For transmission, they would 
need to seek open, access in transmission by applyi ng to the CTU/ STU for 
connectivity with the regional grid/State grid. The Merchant plants selling their 
power through interconnection with the regional/State grid would form part of 
the national grid network. 
(c) Unlike traditional utilities, Merchant Power Plants  compete for 
customers and absorb the full market risk. There are no guarantees that they have 
a minimum off-take of their output. Typically the risk of a Merchant Power Plant is 
carried on the balance sheet of the promoter. The tariff for the merchant Plants 
would be market determined depending upon the grid conditions and the 
requirements that they meet. These plants would nor mally not enter into long 
term Power Purchase Agreements (PPA). Since these p lants do not carry any 
long term purchase obligations on the part of the buyers, they would essentially 
have to arrive at market determined tariffs acceptable to the buyers. 
Further, the National Electricity Policy and the Ta riff Policy state that 
consumers below poverty line who consume below a specified level, say 30 units 
per month, may receive a special support through cross subsidy. Tariffs for such 
designated group of consumers will be at least 50% of the average cost of 
supply.

deep sea water. After conducting several experiments in the Laboratory (500 Litre per day

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): Mr. Deputy 
Chairman, Sir, all sections of the House should have been allowed to take part in 
the debate on the Bill, The Members are denied an opportunity to take part in this 
Bill and I strongly condemn the attitude of the BJP. They

have held the Parliament to ransom. They cannot deny the Telugu Desam Party, 
the CPI(M), the CPI, the Forward Bloc, the RSP, the Congress party, the NCP 
and all other patrties from taking part. I strongly condemn it. Nevertheless, I want 
to read my reply to the debate which was started by  Shri Yashwant Sinha. 
{Interruptions).  
I am grateful to hon. Shri Yashwant Sinha who opene d the debate on the 
General Budget. He did so in 2004-05 and in 2006-07 too. In 2004-05, as is his 
wont, he found everything wrong with the first Budget of the UPA Government. Not 
one word of praise or acknowledgement of any initiative taken by the Government 
escaped his lips. (Interruptions) That year recorded a growth rate of 7.5 per cent. In 
2006-07, he said that he had a sense of pity for th e Finance Minister and the 
Government. Again, true to his style, not one word acknowledging the impressive 
growth in 2005-06 was uttered during the course of his marathon intervention. 2005-
06 recorded a growth of 9 per cent and 2006-07 is expected to record a growth 
rate of 9.2 per cent. In a way, therefore, the harsh criticism of the Budget by the 
BJP, especially by Shri Yashwant Sinha, is welcome. Such criticism appears to 
bode well for the economy. The more vehement the criticism, the better the growth 
story turns out to be. May I, therefore, wish Shri Yashwant Sinha, many happy 
returns? In the interest of robust and sustained ec onomic growth of the 
country, may I wish him a long life, many more years in the opposition and many 
more speeches opposing the Budget? [Interruptions)  
The Budget may not have satisfied everyone, but there are surely aspects of the 
Budget which have been universally acclaimed. Why h ave these escaped the 
attention of Shri Sinha? I think, only an extremely churlish Opposition can find 
no merit at all in the Budget. (Interruptions)  
Let me deal with the issue that is uppermost in the  minds of most hon. 
Members and that is inflation. If you agree with th e views shared by most 
economists, inflation is a monetary phenomenon. Loo k at the monetary 
aggregates: money supply is growing at 21 per cent.  Non-food credit has 
increased, year on year, by 30 per cent. There are large inflows of foreign 
exchange For exampie, in 2005-06, the remittances alone from Indians working 
overseas have been estimated at over USS 24 billion. So far, this year, we have 
added US$ 42 billion, including valuation change, to the reserves. Besides, the 
high growth of the economy is fuelling demand, 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2007] 
and supply of many items has not been able to keep pace with demand (Interruptions)  
The current inflation is driven largely by the primary articles group. In the last few weeks, 
the contributors to Inggation have been: maize, vegetable oils, fish, groundnut, atta, rice bran 
oil, cement and some items of steel, electrical machinery and wires and cables. We had a 
similar situation of inflationary pressures in 1990-91,1998-99 and in 2002-03 As the supply 
of primary articles improved, inflation moderated subsequently I wish to draw the attention 
of the hon. Members to the supply side of some essential primary articles For example, except in 
1999-2000, wheat production has stagnated between 66 million and 72 million tonnes 
during the lest 10 years, (interruptions)  
Rice production has remaned between 81 million and 90 million tonnes during most of the 
ten years period. The production of pulses has not exceeded 14.9 million tonnes. 
Demand for each of these items is rising every year. The only long-term answer is to 
increase production and productivity. ..(Interruptions)...  
Since inflation is a monetary phenomenon, RBI has the direct responsibility for 
maintaining price stability. When I met with t he Central Board of the RBI recently, I pointed 
out that Government had been fully supportive of the RBI in the measures that had taken and 
urged the RBS to continue to be Vigilant and take such measures as are necessary & maintain 
price stability. The RBI has already taken a number of steps to moderate money supply. 5t 
has used instruments such as the repo rate, the MSS arsdCRR These monetary steps will 
temper core inflation over a period of time. ...(interruptions)....  
However, I may also note that monetary steps do not have the same impact on fuel 
and food items. For example, when crude oil prices nit US$ 75 a barrel, the only way we 
could provide a cushion to the people was to absorb a large part of the price rise on \the 
Budget and on the balance sheets of the oil companies. Subsequently, there was a 
supply-demand mismatch in sugar. This was followed by supply constraints in wheat and 
puises The long-term answer is to produce more in order to meet the rising demand In 
the short term, we can only reduce customs duties as well as import these items to the 
extent they are available in the world market And that is what we did. Customs dudes were 
cut sharply 
204 

[19 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
We imported 55 lakh tonnes of wheat to augment supplies in the domestic market We have 
allowed import of pulses, edible oils, etc. at nil or low duties. We also curtailed exports 
of some essential commodities, lt is because of these steps that inflation has been 
contained at the current level. The average inflation for 2006-07 is expected to be about 5 
4 per cent ...(Interruptons),,.  
Let me recall another period of high inflation in recent times. It was 2000-01. For 48 
out of 52 week in that year inflation was over 6 per cent, in 22 of those weeks, inflation was 
over 7 per cent and in 12 of those weeks, it was over 8 per cent The principal contributor 
to inflation in that year was fuel and power WPI inflation touched a high of 8.8 per cent in the 
week ending January 13,2001 and average inflation for 2000-01 was 7.2 percent Inflation 
was moderated by the Government over the next six t o twelve months. 
.(Interruptions)..,  
On February 28,2001, Shri Yashwant Sinha rose to pr esent the Budget 
for 2001-02. The year 2000-01 was drawing to a clos e and inflation was 
still above 7:5 per cent What did the Finance Minis ter have to say about 
inflation? How many words in his speech were devote d to inflation? Hon. 
Members may be surprised to know that the only sent ence on inflation in 
that speech occurs in paragraph Sand it consists of  11 words, and these 
words were "Inflation, excluding energy, was around  4 per cent during the 
year." Not a word about WPI. Not a word of explanat ion why inflation 
should be measured excluding energy suppose I repor t inflation excluding 
primary articles, would that be acceptable to this House? In fact, the most 
callous treatment of the worst period of inflation was in the Budget Speech 
delivered on February 28,2001 ........ (Interruption)..  
Mr. Y ashwant Sinha, apparently, sees no connection between moderating inflation and 
impacting growth, ft seems to me that he is inviting Government to take the wrong course that 
will effectively kill growth. After 2000-01, the year of high inflation, the fiscal and monetary 
steps taken by the NDA Government effectively pushed down growth to an average of 4.66 
percent in three years. We do not intend to commit the mistake. In fact the record of Mr. 
Yashwant Sinha in terms of GDP growth rate, fiscal deficit and revenue deficit is the 
worst in recent years. In the five years that he was Finance Minister of the NDA 
Government the average GDP growth rate was 5.32 per cent He inherited a fiscal deficit of 
4.8 per cent and when he left office, the fiscal deficit had increased to 5 9 per cent in 2002-
03. He

years — in promoting growth or reining in the fiscal deficit or the revenue deficit. 
...(Interruptions)....  
The difference between 2000-01 and 2006-07 is that,  in 2000-01, we 
had high inflation but modest growth. In that year,  GDP grew by only 4.4 
per cent. In 2006-07, GDP is growing at over 9 per cent. As the Prime
